headline: weak
texts: Several core objectives need rebuilding, and that is useful information, not a verdict. Obstruction rewards a few anchors: the level of the block, strangulation signs, and the rule that resuscitation comes first. Start with the review cards flagged below, in the order shown, and redo the module after a day.

You are giving one most-common-cause for every setting. Redo the PYQ-versus-current-practice card, then say it aloud: PYQs expected hernia in India, adhesions lead wherever abdominal surgery is common, carcinoma leads in large bowel.

Causes are sitting in your head as an unsorted list. Rebuild it with three boxes: intraluminal (impaction, gallstone, bezoar), intramural (tumour, stricture, atresia, intussusception), extramural (adhesions, hernia, volvulus, external compression).

The timeline of features is not yet logical for you. Ask how much bowel lies beyond the block. High block: vomiting early, distension minimal, constipation late. Large bowel block: constipation and distension early, vomiting late. Redo the features card.

You are missing strangulation cues. Constant severe pain, tachycardia, fever, localised guarding and raised lactate mean ischaemic bowel, not simple obstruction. Reread the strangulation card and look for the changed pain word in every vignette.
Plain-film reading is partly secure. Valvulae conniventes cross the full width in central small bowel; haustra do not in peripheral large bowel. The 3-6-9 numbers run small bowel, colon, caecum.

You are stopping at the first test or the therapeutic one. Write the ladder: plain film first, contrast CT for level, cause and strangulation, ultrasound for a child with intussusception. Barium by mouth is unsafe in perforation or large bowel obstruction.
The signs are mixed together in your memory. Make a four-column card: sign, disease, test, one-line cue. Coffee bean, bird's beak, claw, target and Rigler's triad each get one row.

The management sequence is out of order for you. Redo it as a flowchart: resuscitate, check for strangulation, hernia or closed loop, then trial, then the 24-hour contrast check and the 72-hour limit. The old dictum is quoted but current practice differs.

Hernia risk and eponyms need a rebuild. Risk follows the neck, not frequency: femoral strangulates most. Then a three-line card: Richter equals partial wall, Littre equals Meckel's, Maydl equals W-shaped loop.
Intussusception management is partly secure. A stable child without peritonitis gets image-guided enema reduction; an adult usually has a lead point, often a tumour, so resection is chosen.

Site and bowel state are not yet driving your treatment choice. Sigmoid and viable: detorse and later colectomy. Gangrene or caecum: resect. Right colon cancer: right hemicolectomy. Left: Hartmann's. The caecum perforates first because it is widest.

These one-line answers are partly secure. Gallstone ileus: enterolithotomy. Ogilvie's: correct the cause and electrolytes, then neostigmine with cardiac monitoring. Paralytic ileus: correct potassium, drip and suck.

You reached for adhesions first, then held both answers. That is the right fix, but the habit returns under time pressure. Read the setting words: for an India or developing-countries PYQ, hernia; for current practice, adhesions.
You applied the child's enema to an adult, then recovered. Under exam pressure, ask first: is there a lead point? An adult usually has one, often a tumour, so the answer is resection.

You went to theatre first, then recognised that a stable child gets reduction. Under pressure the safe-feeling choice returns, so run the screen each time: peritonitis, perforation, shock, failed reduction.
You stopped at a familiar test, then rebuilt the ladder. Remember: X-ray shows that it is obstructed, CT shows why. Under pressure the first test pulls hard.

You blended two signs, then separated them. Hold the pairs: coffee bean is sigmoid volvulus on plain film; kidney-shaped caecum goes towards the left upper quadrant; claw on enema, target on ultrasound.
You swapped the markers, then fixed it. Keep the rule simple: valvulae cross the whole width in small bowel; haustra stop short in the large bowel.
You shuffled the numbers, then reanchored them. Under pressure, think calibre: 3 small bowel, 6 colon, 9 caecum, widening distally.
You equated the commonest hernia with the most dangerous, then corrected. Read the exact qualifier: 'most common' is not 'most likely to strangulate'.
You first expected a classic complete obstruction picture, then adjusted. Richter strangulates part of the wall without obstructing; do not wait for vomiting.
You filled the grid wrongly, then derived it. Keep deriving: ask how much bowel lies beyond the block.
You thought silence meant a block, then reversed it. Mechanical obstruction is loud and tinkling; a silent abdomen suggests ileus or late peritonitis.
You applied one volvulus rule, then added site and bowel state. Under pressure: viable sigmoid, scope then colectomy; gangrene or caecum, resect.
You read persistent colic as simple, then recognised strangulation. Under pressure, look for the word constant plus tachycardia or guarding.
You offered a conservative trial where it was unsafe, then corrected. Screen first; the 72-hour trial belongs only to uncomplicated adhesive obstruction.
You reached for theatre first, then reordered. Drip, suck and catheter come before any decision about operating.
You used one cancer operation, then used the site. Right: hemicolectomy with anastomosis. Left: Hartmann's, or selected anastomosis, with a stent as a bridge.
You first named adhesions, then checked the history line. Keep that order under pressure: scars first. No previous surgery makes adhesions unlikely and points to hernia, then tumour.
You mixed up the timings, then anchored them. Timeline: 24 hours contrast check, 24 to 48 hours second look, 72 hours trial limit.
You stretched 'common' to 'most common', then corrected. Cause: carcinoma. Volvulus site: sigmoid. Perforation site: caecum.
You sorted by name, then used wall relation. For any cause ask: inside the lumen, in the wall, or outside it?

You tend to skip the qualifier in the stem: surgical history, age, setting, side of the colon, or the pain change. Underline it before choosing, and ask what the answer would be on the other side of it.

You tend to get the order wrong, often reaching for theatre or a rule before the screen. Say the sequence aloud: resuscitate, check for strangulation, hernia and closed loop, then decide on trial or operation.

You tend to merge look-alikes: signs, folds and eponyms stored as one group. Fix it with side-by-side cards that name the single discriminating feature, such as folds crossing the lumen or not, or the test on which a sign is seen.
You tend to swap numbers. Attach each figure to a meaning, such as 3-6-9 to bowel calibre, or 24, 24 to 48 and 72 hours to the decision each governs, then retest them in application questions.

You tend to stretch a superlative beyond its qualifier. Commonest cause, commonest site, most likely to strangulate and most likely to perforate are different questions. Write the exact qualifier beside each answer.
You tend to reverse a mechanism: which end empties, or whether a blocked gut is loud or silent. Trace what happens above and below the block before filling any table.

You tapped Sure on several answers that were wrong. Those are the most valuable errors in this module, because a corrected confident error sticks best. Before tapping Sure, name the qualifier that decides the answer. Review the cards for those traps first.

You used no hints, even on the questions you missed. A hint after a first miss costs less than a second wrong answer and gives you a different angle on the stem. Use one the next time you are stuck, then compare what it changed.

Work through the cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky objectives. Review them at 1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days. Redo the module in a week; the traps you fell into are the ones the exam is most likely to set again.
